name: Ledger Replication
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Keeping a Thousand Copies in Sync
lesson.summary: Ledger replication is the process by which every node in a distributed ledger receives and applies the same updates, so that all the independent copies stay identical over time.
lesson.body:
A distributed ledger is only useful if the copies it distributes actually match. Having a hundred nodes each holding a different version of "the truth" is not a feature, it is a failure. Ledger replication is the mechanism, or really the set of mechanisms, that keeps every node's copy of the ledger identical, or at least converging toward identical, as new transactions arrive.

This builds directly on the distributed ledger concept, but it answers the question that concept leaves open: how, mechanically, do updates travel from wherever they originate to every node that needs them? And it builds on distributed systems more broadly, because replication is a general problem in computing, not one invented for blockchains. Database engineers have replicated data across multiple servers for decades, long before anyone wrote the word blockchain, to protect against server failure and to let users in different regions read data from a nearby copy instead of a distant one.

There are two broad strategies worth knowing. In active replication, every node independently receives the same input, in this case new transactions, and independently computes the same result, so the copies stay in sync because they all did the same work. In passive replication, one node processes an update first and then sends the already computed result to the others, who simply apply it. Public blockchains lean toward something closer to active replication: nodes broadcast transactions to their peers, and each node independently validates and applies them according to the same rules, rather than blindly copying a leader's output.

The hard part is not sending the data, networks are good at that. The hard part is handling the moments when copies temporarily disagree, because messages arrive in different orders at different nodes, or because two nodes each produce a valid looking update at nearly the same time, or because a node was briefly offline and missed several updates entirely. A ledger with a thousand nodes spread across the world cannot guarantee that a message sent from one reaches all 999 others in the same instant, so any honest design has to assume brief, ordinary disagreement is normal and build a process for resolving it, rather than pretending it cannot happen.

This is worth taking seriously rather than glossing over, because it is where a lot of blockchain marketing gets vague. "The ledger is replicated across the network" sounds tidy, but replication under real network conditions, with delayed messages, temporarily offline nodes, and even dishonest participants, is the actual engineering problem that consensus mechanisms exist to solve. Replication is the plumbing; consensus, covered elsewhere in this course, is what decides which version of a temporarily disputed ledger becomes the one everyone replicates going forward, so that the whole network eventually settles back on one shared, agreed-upon copy.
